en: The Theravāda Vinaya Mahāvibhaṅga:
The Section on Forfeiture (Nissaggiyakaṇḍa)
The Chapter on the Pairs 27.
The Training Rule on the Great Weavers.
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, a certain man, about to go on a journey, said this to his wife: “Take this thread and give it to such-and-such a weaver; have him weave a robe and set it aside.
When I have returned, I will clothe the venerable Upananda with it.
A certain monk who was wandering for alms heard these words being spoken by that man.
Then that bhikkhu approached the Venerable Upananda the Sakyaputta; having approached, he said this to the Venerable Upananda the Sakyaputta: “Friend Upananda, you are one of great merit!
In such-and-such a place, a certain man, while departing on a journey, said to his wife:
‘Having taken the yarn, give it to such-and-such a weaver; have him weave a robe and set it aside, for when I have returned, I will clothe the noble Upananda with it.’”
“There is, friends, that attendant of mine.
That weaver was indeed the attendant of the Venerable Upananda the Sakyan-son.
Then the Venerable Upananda the Sakyan-son went to where that weaver was; having approached, he said this to that weaver:
“Friend, this robe-cloth is being woven for me; make it long and wide. Make it well-stretched, well-woven, well-beaten, well-scrubbed, and well-carded.
“Venerable sir, these people have given me the thread;
weave the robe-cloth with this thread.”
“Venerable sir, it is not possible to make it long, wide, or thick.
But, venerable sir, it is possible to make it well-woven, well-stretched, well-combed, and well-carded.
“Come now, friend, make it long, wide, and thick.”
“It will not be bound with that thread.
Then the weaver, having wound the thread he had brought onto the loom, approached the woman; having approached her, he said to her, “Madam, I have need of thread.
“Did you not tell me, noble sir, ‘Weave a robe with this thread’?”
“Truly, noble lady, you told me: ‘Remove the robe-cloth with this thread.
But Master Upananda said to me: ‘Come now, friend, stretch it out and widen it;
it will not be held together by that thread.’”
Then that woman gave back as much thread as she had first received.
The Venerable Upananda the Sakyan son heard: “It seems that man has returned from his journey.
Then the Venerable Upananda the Sakyan son went to that man’s residence; having arrived, he...
He sat down on the prepared seat.
Then that man approached the Venerable Upananda the Sakyan son; having approached, he paid homage to the Venerable Upananda the Sakyan son and sat down to one side.
Sitting there, the man said this to his wife: “Is your robe finished?”
“Venerable sir, that robe has been washed.
“Bring it, noble lady; we shall clothe the Venerable Upananda with the robe.
Then that woman brought out the robe, gave it to her husband, and reported this matter to him.
Then that man, having given the robe to the Venerable Upananda the son of the Sakyans, complained, grumbled, and became indignant, saying:
"These ascetics, the sons of the Sakyans, have great desires and are not contented.
It is not easy to clothe them with robes."
"How indeed could the venerable Upananda, without having been previously invited by me, approach weavers and make a choice regarding a robe?
The monks heard that man complaining, grumbling, and resenting this.
Those monks who were few in desires... [and so on]... they complained, grumbled, and resented it, saying:
“How indeed could the venerable Upananda the Sakyaputta, without having been previously invited, approach a householder’s weaver and specify the kind of robe he desires?
Then those monks, having rebuked the venerable Upananda the Sakyaputta in many ways, reported this matter to the Blessed One. … [The Blessed One asked:
“Is it true, Upananda, that you, without having been previously invited, approached a householder’s weaver and specified the kind of robe you desired?”
“It is true, Blessed One.
“Is he a kinsman of yours, Upananda, or a stranger?
“He is a stranger, Blessed One.”
“An unrelated person, foolish man, does not know what is appropriate or inappropriate, or what is proper or improper for another unrelated person.
Yet you, foolish man, having previously been uninvited, have approached an unrelated householder’s weaver and made demands regarding a robe.
This, foolish man, will not lead to the confidence of those without confidence... [and so on].”
And furthermore, monks, you should recite this training rule as follows:

“If an unrelated householder or housewife should have a robe woven by weavers for the sake of a monk, and if that monk, not having been previously invited, should approach those weavers and specify the kind of robe he desires, saying:
‘Friends, this robe is being woven for me; make it long and wide; make it well-stretched, well-woven, well-beaten, well-scratched, and well-carded.’”
‘Perhaps we too might give something, however small, to the venerable ones.
And if that monk, having spoken thus, should give something, even if it is merely a portion of alms-food, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.
Regarding the phrase “but having designated a monk”:
For the sake of a monk, having made a monk the object [of his thought], he desires to clothe that monk.
One who is unrelated (*aññātaka*) means one who is not connected by blood through the mother’s side or the father’s side, up to the seventh generation of ancestors.
A householder (*gahapati*) is anyone who dwells in a home.
A housewife (*gahapatānī*) is...
"Whoever dwells in a house" refers to anyone living in a home.
"By weavers" means by cloth-makers.
"Robe" means any one of the six kinds of robes, the last of which is suitable for assignment.
"Should have woven" means...
"He causes it to be removed. In that context,
"that monk" refers to the monk for whose sake the robe-cloth is being woven.
"Previously uninvited" means he has not been told before:
"Venerable sir, what kind of robe-cloth do you need? What kind of robe-cloth shall I have woven for you?
Having approached the weavers...
Having gone home, having approached anyone at all:
"He would make a formal request regarding the robe-cloth" means:
"Friend, this robe-cloth is being woven for me; make it long and wide."
“Make it well-applied, well-stretched, well-beaten, well-scratched, and well-polished.
Perhaps we too might give you, venerable sirs, some small gift.
And having spoken thus, that bhikkhu might give something, even if it were merely a portion of almsfood.
"Alms-food" means:
whether it be rice-gruel, cooked rice, fresh food, a lump of flour, a tooth-stick, or even a thread for a bandage; at the very least, he speaks the Dhamma.
By his speech, he causes [the robe] to be lengthened, broadened, or made fitted; in the act of doing so, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
By the mere acquisition, it becomes an offense entailing relinquishment (nissaggiya).
It must be relinquished to either the Saṅgha, a group, or an individual.
And thus, monks, should it be relinquished:
… [as before] … “Venerable sir, this robe-cloth of mine, which I had previously approached an unrelated weaver of a householder and specified the kind of robe I desired, is to be relinquished.
I relinquish it to the Saṅgha. … [as before] …
"May he give," ... "may they give," ... "I give to the Venerable One."

If, perceiving one who is unrelated as unrelated, he approaches a weaver who is a householder and, without having been previously invited, makes a request regarding a robe, it is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya pācittiya).

If, being uncertain whether one is unrelated, he approaches a weaver who is a householder and, without having been previously invited, makes a request regarding a robe, it is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.

If, perceiving one who is unrelated as related, he approaches a weaver who is a householder and, without having been previously invited, makes a request regarding a robe, it is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.
If one perceives a relative as a non-relative, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If one is doubtful regarding a relative, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If one perceives a relative as a relative, there is no offense.
There is no offense:
[if it is] for kinsmen,
or [if they have already] invited [one].
If, for the sake of another,

one causes a low-value item to be woven by means of one's own wealth when that person wishes to have a high-value item woven; or, [if one causes a high-value item to be woven] when that person wishes to have a low-value item woven.
"In the case of one who is insane,
or in the case of the first offender.
The seventh training rule concerning the chief weaver is concluded.
